Not every installed package ships to production. See which ones do.

A vulnerability scanner lists packages your deployed app never loads. Drop in a package-lock.json and see the lockfile evidence for which dependencies actually reach production versus which are build- or test-only — entirely in your browser.

Drag a package-lock.json here, or

— or paste its contents below —

Don't have one handy? — a small lockfile with production, transitive-production, and build-only packages, so you can see the report shape before using your own.

What this is and isn't

  • Everything runs in your browser. The lockfile you drop or paste is never uploaded — there is no server here to send it to.
  • "Build-only" is a lockfile classification, not a security verdict. A build-only package can still run on the machine that builds your app, and dynamic imports or other runtime behavior need human review — this cannot prove absence, only report what the lockfile states.
  • This reads package-lock.json v2/v3 (npm 7+) only. It does not inspect yarn or pnpm lockfiles.
  • Only anonymous, aggregate usage counts (for example "a report was generated") may be recorded locally — never the lockfile contents or package names.

Common questions

Does "build-only" mean this package is safe to ignore?

No. Build-only means the lockfile shows every install location for that package as dev-only — absent from your deployed application artifact. It can still be exposed on the machine that runs your build, and a scanner flagging it there is doing its job. Use this report to prioritize review, not to dismiss a finding.

Why does a package I didn't install show up?

Most entries are transitive: a dependency your direct dependencies pulled in. The Evidence column says why each row was classified the way it was — "declared by the application" for packages in your own package.json, or "at least one install location is on a production path" for a transitive dependency that a production package needs.

Does this replace my vulnerability scanner?

No. This tool never checks packages against any advisory database — it only reads what your lockfile already states about where each package installs. Pair it with your existing scanner's findings to see which flagged packages are actually reachable in production.

Is my lockfile uploaded anywhere?

No. Parsing happens with JavaScript running in your own browser tab. This page makes no network request with your file's contents — there is nothing to intercept because nothing is sent. Only anonymous, aggregate usage counts like "a report was generated" may be recorded locally, with an opt-out below.

Is there a command-line version?

Yes — the same classification logic ships as a local Python CLI (npm_deployment_evidence.py) in this tool's repository, for CI pipelines or scripted use. See the README for its usage.

Does this work with yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml?

No. This reads package-lock.json v2 or v3 only — the format npm 7 and later writes. Drop or paste a yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml and you'll get an error asking for package-lock.json instead, because the two formats don't share a structure this tool can read. If your project uses npm but the lockfile predates v2, delete it and run npm install again to regenerate a version this report can parse.

Which npm vulnerabilities actually reach production? · This tool vs. npm audit

vs-npm-audit.html.text:
← npm deployment evidence

This tool vs. npm audit

npm audit is the vulnerability scanner almost every npm project already has — it ships inside npm itself, no separate install, and it is very likely the tool that produced the finding count you are looking at right now. It checks every package in your lockfile against GitHub's public security advisory database and reports which ones have a known issue, at which severity, and whether a fix is available.

That makes npm audit the right tool for one job: finding out whether a package in your dependency tree has a known vulnerability. This tool does not do that job and has no advisory database of its own — it never checks a package name against anything. What it does is answer the question npm audit's own output leaves open: of the packages it just flagged, which ones does your lockfile show reaching your deployed application, and which exist only for a build, test, or lint step to run.

What we actually ran

Rather than describe npm audit from memory, this page is built from running it: npm 10.9.7, a throwaway project with one vulnerable production dependency (minimatch) and one vulnerable devDependency (minimist), npm install, then npm audit --json. The full output is reproducible with the same two packages at the same versions. 

{
  "vulnerabilities": {
    "minimatch": { "name": "minimatch", "severity": "high", "isDirect": true,
      "via": [ … ], "range": "<=3.1.3", "nodes": ["node_modules/minimatch"],
      "fixAvailable": { … } },
    "minimist": { "name": "minimist", "severity": "critical", "isDirect": true,
      "via": [ … ], "range": "<=0.2.3", "nodes": ["node_modules/minimist"],
      "fixAvailable": { … } }
  },
  "metadata": {
    "vulnerabilities": { "high": 1, "critical": 1, "total": 2 },
    "dependencies": { "prod": 5, "dev": 1, "total": 5 }
  }
}

minimist exists only in devDependencies in that project. It is reported exactly the same shape as minimatch, the production dependency — name, severity, isDirect, via, range, nodes, fixAvailable. Nothing on that finding says "dev." The only place the run distinguishes prod from dev at all is the aggregate count at the bottom, metadata.dependencies — a total, not a per-finding label.

Re-running with npm audit --omit=dev does remove minimist from the report and drops the critical count from 1 to 0 — npm audit can scope to production. But it does so by excluding the dev-only finding, not by keeping it and marking it dev-only. A reviewer who wants to see both — what's on the production path and what's dev-only, each labelled, in one document — has to run the audit twice, with and without the flag, and diff the two lists by hand. That is the exact manual step this tool's report replaces: it reads the same lockfile once and classifies every entry — declared by the application, reachable only through a production dependency, or build-only — with the evidence for each classification, in one exportable Markdown or JSON file.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Does this package in my lockfile have a known vulnerability? npm audit — it checks against a live advisory database this tool does not have.
Of the packages npm audit just flagged, which ones does my deployed application actually load? This tool — drop in the same package-lock.json and read the production/build-only split, with the reason for each row.
I want a document I can attach to a security questionnaire showing the classification, not just a console count. This tool's Markdown or JSON export. npm audit's JSON is a point-in-time advisory list without that reasoning.
Is a build-only finding safe to ignore? Neither tool says yes. A compromised build or test dependency still runs on your machine and in CI — see the FAQ below.

Open the free lockfile evidence tool

Common questions

Should I use this tool or npm audit?

Both, for different questions. npm audit checks the packages in your lockfile against a vulnerability advisory database (GitHub Security Advisories) and tells you which ones have a known issue. It does not tell you, on a per-finding basis, whether the affected package reaches your deployed application or only exists for your build and test tooling. This tool answers that second question by reading what the lockfile already records about each package's install path, and produces a report you can attach to the audit output.

Doesn't npm audit already separate production from dev dependencies?

Partly. npm audit --json reports an aggregate count of prod versus dev dependencies scanned (the metadata.dependencies object), and npm audit --omit=dev will exclude devDependencies from the run entirely. But run against a real project (verified on npm 10.9.7 with a lockfile containing one vulnerable production dependency and one vulnerable devDependency), the per-finding objects in vulnerabilities carry no field marking a specific finding as production-path or dev-only — only name, severity, isDirect, via, range, nodes and fixAvailable. And --omit=dev removes dev-only findings from the report rather than keeping and labelling them, so a reviewer who wants to see and document which findings are dev-only, not just hide them, has to run the audit twice and diff the two lists by hand. That manual diff is what this tool's report replaces.

Is this affiliated with npm, Inc. or the npm CLI project?

No. npm audit is named here only to describe what it does and does not report, based on running it directly (npm 10.9.7, npm audit --json) and its own --help output. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by npm, Inc. or the Node.js Foundation.

See also: Which npm vulnerabilities actually reach production?

No warranty. This free page is not security, legal, or compliance advice, and it does not certify that an application is secure, unaffected, or compliant. It reports what a lockfile records about dependency paths; a lockfile can be out of date, and reachability in the dependency graph is not the same as reachability of vulnerable code at runtime. Verify with a qualified professional before relying on it in an audit or a customer response. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage arising from its use.

which-npm-vulnerabilities-actually-reach.text:
← npm deployment evidence

Which npm vulnerabilities actually reach production?

npm audit returns 94 findings and a customer's security questionnaire asks whether your deployed application is affected. The honest answer needs a distinction the audit output does not draw: which of those packages your running application actually loads, and which exist only so that your tests, bundler, linter and type checker can run.

Open the free lockfile evidence tool

The lockfile already knows

A package-lock.json (v2 or v3) records, for every installed package, whether it was reached only through devDependencies. npm marks those entries dev: true. Anything reachable from your declared runtime dependencies — directly or transitively — is not marked, and a package reached by both paths counts as production, because it is.

That single flag is the evidence behind "this finding is in our test runner." It is already in the file you have; it is just not what a headline audit count shows you.

Why the distinction is worth drawing

  • Triage order. A vulnerability in code your users execute is not the same priority as one in a linter plugin.
  • Answering questionnaires honestly. "94 findings, 11 of which are on the production path" is a truthful and far more useful answer than either "94" or "none of them matter."
  • An artifact you can hand over. A dated report showing how the classification was made is reviewable. A verbal assertion that "most of those are dev" is not.

What it does not mean

A dev-only finding is not a finding you can ignore. Build and test dependencies execute on developer machines and in CI, where they can reach source code, environment variables, and deployment credentials — a path that real supply-chain attacks have used repeatedly. The classification changes the question being answered: whether your deployed application is affected is not the same question as whether your pipeline is.

How to use it

  1. Drag package-lock.json into the page, or paste its contents. Parsing runs in your browser — the file is never uploaded, and there is no server to upload it to.
  2. Read the split: production-path dependencies, and the ones npm marks dev-only.
  3. Download the Markdown or JSON report and attach it to the audit output or the questionnaire response.

The same classification rules are available as a CLI in the repository, so the check can run in CI on every change rather than only when someone asks. The tool has no vulnerability database and makes no network calls; it adds reachability context to a scanner's output rather than replacing it.

Common questions

Which npm vulnerabilities actually reach production?

Only the ones on the production dependency path — the packages reachable from your declared dependencies rather than from devDependencies. A lockfile records this: npm marks dev-only entries with a dev flag, and a package reachable from both paths is not dev-only. Separating the two usually shrinks a frightening audit count substantially, because test runners, bundlers, linters and type tooling pull in a large share of a typical dependency tree and none of it is shipped to users.

Does a dev-only dependency mean the vulnerability does not matter?

No. It means the exposure is different, not absent. A compromised build or test dependency runs on developer machines and in CI, where it can read source, secrets and tokens — that is a real and serious risk, and supply-chain attacks have repeatedly used exactly that path. What the distinction changes is triage order and the honest answer to 'is our deployed application affected', which is a different question from 'is our build pipeline affected'.

Is this a security scanner?

No, and it deliberately does not try to be. It reads a package-lock.json you supply and reports which dependencies reach the production path and which npm marks dev-only. It has no vulnerability database, makes no network calls, and never uploads the lockfile. Use it to give a scanner's output the reachability context it lacks, not to replace the scanner.

It reports what a lockfile records about dependency paths; a lockfile can be out of date, and reachability in the dependency graph is not the same as reachability of vulnerable code at runtime. Verify with a qualified professional before relying on it in an audit or a customer response.
